kingfisher_study_abstract: This study includes sequencing data from Bacillus anthracis strains isolated during an outbreak of anthrax on the Yamal Peninsula in the summer of 2016 and independently in Yakutia in 2015. A common feature of these strains is their conservation in permafrost, from which they were extracted either due to the thawing of permafrost (Yamal strains) or as the result of paleontological excavations (Yakut strains). All strains isolated on the Yamal share an identical genotype belonging to lineage B.Br.001/002, pointing to a common source of infection in a territory over 250 km in length. In contrast, during the excavation in Yakutia, three genetically different strains were recovered from a single pit. One strain belongs to B.Br.001/002, as the Yamal strains. Despite the remoteness of Yamal from Yakutia, whole genome sequence analysis showed that the B.Br.001/002 strains are very closely related. The two other strains contribute to two different branches of A.Br.008/011, one of the remarkable polytomies described so far in the B. anthracis population. The geographic distribution of the strains belonging to this polytomy is suggesting that this polytomy emerged in the thirteenth century, in combination with the constitution of a unified Mongol empire extending from China to Eastern Europe. We propose an evolutionary model for B. anthracis recent evolution in which the B lineage spread throughout Eurasia and was subsequently replaced by the A lineage except in some geographically isolated areas. See report in biorxiv https://doi.org/10.1101/486290

Knowledge of the genotypes of circulating strains is important for epidemiological monitoring at the local and global levels. Full-genomic sequencing and subsequent analysis of single nucleotide polymorphisms is the method of genotyping with the highest resolutions of a powerful phylogenetic ability.To study the genotypes and genomic features of the causative agents of anthrax and tularemia circulating in Kazakhstan with using of highly discriminatory methods and full genomic sequencing.

kingfisher_study_title: Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis Raw sequence reads
kingfisher_study_abstract: Background: Metabarcoding of invertebrate derived DNA (iDNA) is increasingly used to describe vertebrate diversity in terrestrial ecosystems. Fly iDNA has also shown potential as a tool for detecting pathogens. Combining these approaches make fly iDNA a promising tool for understanding the ecology and distribution of novel pathogens or emerging infectious diseases.Aims and Methods: We used fly iDNA to explore the geographical distribution of Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis (Bcbva) along a gradient from the forest within Tai National Park (TNP), Ivory Coast, out to surrounding villages. We tested fly pools (N=100 pools of 5 flies) collected in the forest (N=25 pools), along the forest edge (N=50 pools), and near surrounding villages (N=25 pools) for Bcbva. Using the same iDNA, we sought to reconstruct fly and mammal communities with metabarcoding, with the aim of investigating potential links with Bcbva detection.Results: We detected Bcbva in 5 / 100 fly pools and positivity varied significantly across the habitat types (forest = 4 / 25, edge = 1 / 50, village = 0 / 25). It was possible to culture Bcbva from all positive fly pools, confirming their positivity, while sequencing of their whole genomes revealed a considerable portion of known genomic diversity for this pathogen. iDNA generated data about the mammal and fly communities in these habitats, revealing the highest mammal diversity in the forest and considerable changes in fly community composition along the gradient. Bcbva host range estimates from fly iDNA were largely identical to the results of long term carcass monitoring efforts in the region.Conclusion: We show that fly iDNA can generate data on the geographic distribution and host range of a pathogen at kilometer scales, as well as reveal the phylogenetic diversity of pathogen. Our results highlight the power of fly iDNA for mammal biomonitoring and pathogen surveillance.

kingfisher_study_title: Rapid identification of microbial pathogens and antimicrobial resistance from bloodstream infections using long-read sequencing
kingfisher_study_abstract: The gold standard for bloodstream infection (BSI) diagnostics involves culturing positive blood cultures (BC) using phenotypic methods for organism identification and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) testing, which can take up to five days. However, it is crucial to optimize antimicrobial therapy as soon as possible to reduce morbidity and mortality. We present a novel laboratory and bioinformatic workflow to rapidly identify bacterial and fungal organisms and AMR determinants from positive BCs using Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing. This repository contains the Illumina sequencing data from matching pure isolates.

kingfisher_design_description: Bacterial genomic DNA was extracted with the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Genomic DNA Isolation kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturers instructions. Next-generation sequencing was performed at Fiocruz Platform Network (Oswaldo Cruz Institute, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) using an Illumina NextSeq 2000 sequencer (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). The preparation of libraries for sequencing was carried out using the Nextera DNA Flex kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) following the manufacturers instructions, and the sequencing run was performed with P2 XLEAP-SBSTM Kit reagents (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA), with 300 cycles (2  151  base pair paired-end), according to the manufacturers recommendations.
kingfisher_submitter: Department of Experimental and Preclinical Develop, Fundacao Oswaldo Cruz
kingfisher_study_title: Bacillus anthracis Genome sequencing
kingfisher_study_abstract: The National Institute for Quality Control in Health is the federal laboratory that analyzes products subject to health surveillance, including food. The Institute of Technology in Immunobiologicals is responsible for producing immunobiologicals to meet the demands of the population. This study aims to develop a machine-learning (ML) Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR) model for differentiating B. cereus species isolated from a pharmaceutical and food industry. One hundred strains identified as belonging to the B. cereus group will be evaluated. The strains were isolated from different food samples (n=50) and from the industry (n=50). Phenotypic characterization will be carried out using the VITEK2 and MALDI Biotyper. Molecular characterization will be carried out by sequencing the 16S rRNA, gyrB and rpoB genes. Strains not identified by these techniques will be subjected to whole genome sequencing and analyzed using various taxonomic approaches. FT-IR analysis will be carried out to develop ML classifiers for differentiating species of the group. The strains identified as B. cereus will be typed by Multilocus sequence typing and an ML classifier will be developed to differentiate the sequence types by FT-IR. The MALDI database will be expanded with unidentified strains and subsequently identified using molecular techniques. The strains will be evaluated for aggregative activity, biofilm production on different surfaces and spore tolerance to disinfectants. Afterwards, dendrograms and Scartter plot graphs with FT-IR profiles will be constructed to evaluate the dispersion of the strains by sample type, production site, the phenotypic characteristics evaluated (biofilm/aggregation) and isolation date. This information will be important for assessing the dispersion of clones within the pharmaceutical industry and in foodstuffs.
